questions.question: What force pulls things down towards the ground?
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth. It is why a dropped ball falls and why we stay on the ground.

questions.question: What force slows down a box as it slides across the floor?
questions.explanation: Friction happens when two surfaces rub together. It is also why your hands feel warm when you rub them fast.

questions.question: Which of these metals does a magnet pick up?
questions.explanation: Iron and steel are magnetic. Gold, aluminium and copper are not, which is why a magnet can sort steel cans from aluminium ones.

questions.question: A straw in a glass of water looks bent. What is this bending of light called?
questions.explanation: Light changes speed and direction when it goes from water into air. This makes things look bent or in the wrong place.

questions.question: What flows through a wire to make a lamp light up?
questions.explanation: A battery pushes electricity round a wire. When it flows through the bulb, the bulb lights up.

questions.question: What do we call the sound that bounces back from a far wall or cliff?
questions.explanation: Sound waves bounce off hard surfaces. Because the sound has to travel there and back, you hear the echo a little later.

questions.question: A shadow is made when an object blocks what?
questions.explanation: Light moves in straight lines. When something stops the light, the dark shape behind it is the shadow.

questions.question: Which unit do scientists use to measure mass?
questions.explanation: A kilogram is 1,000 grams. Metres measure length, litres measure volume and seconds measure time.

questions.question: A see-saw is a simple machine. What kind is it?
questions.explanation: A lever turns around a fixed point called the pivot. On a see-saw, the pivot is in the middle.

questions.question: Which simple machine helps to raise a flag up a flagpole?
questions.explanation: A pulley is a wheel with a rope over it. Pulling down on one side lifts the other side up.

questions.question: What is the word for the energy that moving things have?
questions.explanation: A rolling ball or a running child has kinetic energy. The faster something moves, the more kinetic energy it has.

questions.question: What happens if you push the north poles of two magnets together?
questions.explanation: Two poles that are the same push each other away. A north pole and a south pole pull each other together.

questions.question: Which force slows down a falling parachute?
questions.explanation: The big canopy catches the air and pushes against it. This makes the parachutist fall slowly and land softly.

questions.question: A glass prism can split white light into what?
questions.explanation: White light is a mix of all the colours. A prism bends each colour a little differently, so they spread out.

questions.question: What must an object do to make a sound?
questions.explanation: Sound starts with something shaking very fast back and forth. A guitar string and a drum skin both vibrate when played.

questions.question: Where would you hear no sound, because there is no air to carry it?
questions.explanation: Sound needs something to travel through, like air or water. Outer space is almost empty, so sound cannot travel there.

questions.question: Copper wire lets electricity flow easily. What do we call such a material?
questions.explanation: Metals are good conductors. Plastic and rubber are insulators, so they cover wires and keep us safe.

questions.question: What makes a balloon stick to a wall after you rub it on your jumper?
questions.explanation: Rubbing moves tiny charges from one thing to another. The charged balloon is then pulled towards the wall.

questions.question: Solar panels turn what into electricity?
questions.explanation: Solar panels use light from the Sun. They work best on clear days but also give some power on cloudy days.

questions.question: Which scientist is famous for a story about an apple and gravity?
questions.explanation: The story says Newton saw an apple fall and wondered why. He later described how gravity works for apples and for planets.

questions.question: Which famous scientist with wild white hair developed the theory of relativity?
questions.explanation: Einstein showed that space and time are linked. He was born in Germany and later lived in Switzerland and the USA.

questions.question: What do we call the upward push of water that helps a boat float?
questions.explanation: Water pushes up on anything put into it. A boat floats when this push is as big as the boat's weight.

questions.question: What does a compass needle point towards?
questions.explanation: The needle is a small magnet. It lines up with the Earth's magnetic field, so it shows the way north.

questions.question: What does a magnifying glass do?
questions.explanation: A magnifying glass is a curved lens. It bends light so that small things look larger.

questions.question: Which unit tells us how fast a car is going?
questions.explanation: Speed is how far you go in a certain time. In most of Europe, road signs show speed limits in kilometres per hour.

questions.question: Which spoon gets hot fastest in a bowl of hot soup?
questions.explanation: Metal carries heat very well, so the handle warms up quickly. Wood and plastic carry heat badly.

questions.question: What do we call the path that electricity follows from a battery through a bulb and back?
questions.explanation: Electricity only flows when the path is a complete loop. If there is a gap, the bulb goes out.

questions.question: How does your weight on the Moon compare with your weight on Earth?
questions.explanation: The Moon is much smaller and lighter than the Earth, so its gravity is weaker. You would weigh much less there and could jump higher.

questions.question: Why does a woolly jumper keep you warm?
questions.correct: It traps warm air near your body
wrong: It makes heat all by itself
It rubs your skin to make heat
questions.explanation: Wool holds lots of tiny pockets of air. Air carries heat badly, so your body heat stays in.

questions.question: Which of these makes its own light?
questions.explanation: The Sun is a star that shines by itself. The Moon only looks bright because it reflects light from the Sun.

questions.question: Which simple machine is a playground slide an example of?
questions.explanation: A ramp, or inclined plane, lets things move up or down a slope. It is easier to go up a ramp than to lift straight up.

questions.question: What is the curved piece of glass in a camera or telescope called?
questions.explanation: A lens bends light to make a clear picture. Your eye has a lens inside it too.

questions.question: On a sunny day, which colour of T-shirt gets hottest?
questions.explanation: Dark colours take in more of the Sun's light and turn it into heat. Light colours bounce more of it away.

questions.question: What do we call the stored energy of a ball held high up?
questions.explanation: A ball held up has energy stored because of its height. When you let go, this turns into movement energy.

questions.question: Which scientist is said to have dropped balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa?
questions.explanation: In the story, Galileo showed that heavy and light balls fall at almost the same speed. He lived in Italy about 400 years ago.

questions.question: What do we call how high or low a sound is?
questions.explanation: A tiny whistle makes a high pitch, and a big drum makes a low pitch. Volume is how loud a sound is.

questions.question: Where is a bar magnet's pull the strongest?
questions.explanation: The ends of a magnet are called poles. Dip a bar magnet in paperclips and most stick to the ends.

questions.question: What do we call the rod that a wheel turns around?
questions.explanation: An axle holds a wheel and lets it turn smoothly. Carts, cars and bicycles all use axles.

questions.question: What are the two kinds of electric charge called?
questions.explanation: Opposite charges pull together and the same charges push apart. Electrons carry negative charge.

questions.question: What is the thin wire that glows inside an old-style light bulb called?
questions.explanation: Electricity heats the thin filament until it glows white. Modern LED bulbs make light in a different way and use less energy.

questions.question: About how fast does sound travel through air?
questions.explanation: That is about 1,200 km per hour. It is why you hear a far-away firework bang a few seconds after you see the flash.

questions.question: About how fast does light travel in empty space?
questions.explanation: Light could go round the Earth about seven and a half times in one second. Nothing is known to travel faster.

questions.question: In science, force is measured in which unit?
questions.explanation: One newton is about the force of gravity on a small apple. The unit is named after Isaac Newton.

questions.question: In science, energy is measured in which SI unit?
questions.explanation: Lifting a small apple one metre takes about one joule of energy. The unit honours the English physicist James Joule.

questions.question: The power of a light bulb is measured in which unit?
questions.explanation: A 60-watt old-style bulb uses 60 joules of energy every second. The unit is named after the Scottish engineer James Watt.

questions.question: Which unit is used for frequency, such as how often a sound wave vibrates each second?
questions.explanation: One hertz is one vibration per second. Humans hear sounds from roughly 20 to 20,000 hertz.

questions.question: You lean forward when a bus brakes suddenly. Which idea explains this?
questions.explanation: Things keep moving as they are until a force changes that. Your body wants to keep going forward while the bus slows down.

questions.question: A rocket goes up by pushing hot gas down. Which idea explains this?
questions.explanation: When the rocket pushes gas down, the gas pushes the rocket up. This works even in empty space, where there is no air.

questions.question: On the Moon, an astronaut dropped a hammer and a feather together. What happened?
questions.correct: They landed at the same time
questions.explanation: The Moon has no air to slow the feather down. In a vacuum, all objects fall at the same rate.

questions.question: Which ancient Greek is said to have shouted "Eureka!" in his bath?
questions.explanation: In the story, he saw the water rise as he got in. He realised he could measure the volume of the king's gold crown this way.

questions.question: Which Danish scientist found in 1820 that a wire carrying electricity moves a compass needle?
questions.explanation: Ørsted showed that electricity and magnetism are linked. This led to electric motors and generators.

questions.question: Which colour of visible light has the longest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Red light has the longest waves we can see, and violet has the shortest. Beyond red lies infrared, which we feel as heat.

questions.question: Which three colours of light does a TV or phone screen mix to make its pictures?
questions.explanation: Tiny dots of red, green and blue light mix in your eye. When all three shine fully together, you see white.

questions.question: What do we call the area around a magnet where its force can be felt?
questions.explanation: Iron filings sprinkled near a magnet line up along the field. The Earth also has a magnetic field.

questions.question: How does heat from the Sun reach the Earth through empty space?
questions.explanation: Radiation travels as waves and needs no material to carry it. That is why we feel the Sun's warmth across space.

questions.question: When pasta boils in a pan, which kind of heat transfer moves warm water upwards?
questions.explanation: Warm water is less dense than cold water, so it rises. Cooler water sinks to take its place and a circle of flow forms.

questions.question: Why do wide snowshoes stop you sinking into deep snow?
questions.explanation: The same weight spread over a larger area means less pressure on the snow. That is why you sink less.

questions.question: A knife blade and an axe head are examples of which simple machine?
questions.explanation: A wedge turns a forward push into a force that pushes things apart. A thin edge puts the force on a tiny area, so it cuts easily.

questions.question: A small gear drives a large gear. How does the large gear turn?
questions.explanation: A big gear has more teeth, so it turns fewer times. In return it can turn with more force.

questions.question: Through which of these does sound travel fastest?
questions.explanation: Sound usually moves faster through solids than liquids, and faster through liquids than gases. In steel it is about 15 times faster than in air.

questions.question: Ships use sonar to find the seabed or fish. What does sonar send out?
questions.explanation: Sonar sends a sound pulse and times how long the echo takes to return. This tells the ship how far away something is.

questions.question: What do we call the change in pitch of a siren as an ambulance drives past you?
questions.explanation: The sound waves bunch up as the ambulance comes towards you and spread out as it leaves. So the pitch drops as it passes.

questions.question: Three bulbs are wired in a series circuit. The filament in one breaks. What happens to the other two?
questions.explanation: A series circuit has only one path for the electricity, so one break stops the flow everywhere. In a parallel circuit, the others would stay lit.

questions.question: What does the law of conservation of energy say?
questions.correct: Energy is never created or destroyed
questions.explanation: Energy only changes form, for example from movement to heat. A rolling ball stops because its movement energy becomes heat.

questions.question: Why do steel bridges and some railway tracks have small gaps in them?
questions.correct: To give the steel room to expand
questions.explanation: On hot days steel gets slightly longer. Without the gaps, the metal could bend out of shape.

questions.question: Einstein's equation E = mc² links energy with what?
questions.explanation: It says that a small amount of mass is worth a huge amount of energy. This is the idea behind nuclear power.

questions.question: Which kind of invisible light do most TV remote controls use?
questions.explanation: The remote flashes pulses of infrared light at the TV. A phone camera can often show the flashes even though our eyes cannot.

questions.question: Which invisible light from the Sun can give you sunburn?
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet light has more energy than visible light and can damage skin. Sunscreen and clothes block much of it.

questions.question: The flow of electricity in a wire is measured in which unit?
questions.explanation: The ampere, or amp, tells how much electric charge flows past each second. It is named after the French scientist André-Marie Ampère.

questions.question: What does a fuse do if too much electricity flows through it?
questions.correct: It melts and breaks the circuit
questions.explanation: A thin wire inside the fuse heats up and melts, stopping the current. This protects a device from overheating and fire.

questions.question: Why does a metal handle feel colder than a wooden one at the same temperature?
questions.correct: Metal draws heat from your hand faster
wrong: Metal is always a bit colder
Wood makes a little heat itself
questions.explanation: Both are at room temperature. Metal conducts heat much better, so it pulls warmth from your skin quickly.

questions.question: A periscope lets you see over a wall. What does it use inside?
questions.explanation: Two mirrors bounce the light down a tube, one at the top and one at the bottom. Submarines have long used periscopes to see above the water.

questions.question: What happens to a guitar note if you press the string so the vibrating part is shorter?
questions.explanation: Shorter strings vibrate faster, and faster vibrations make a higher pitch. That is how guitar players play different notes.

questions.question: What do we call it when a sound matches an object's natural vibration and makes it shake strongly?
questions.explanation: A very loud singer can break a thin glass with a note that matches its own vibration. Marching soldiers were told to break step on bridges for this reason.

questions.question: Why do fast trains and racing cars have smooth, rounded shapes?
questions.explanation: A smooth shape lets air flow past easily. Less air resistance means less fuel or electricity is needed.

questions.question: Garage jacks and digger arms use liquid pushed under pressure. What is this system called?
questions.explanation: A liquid can hardly be squeezed, so a small push on a small piston gives a big push on a big piston. This lifts heavy loads.

questions.question: Why does a heavy steel ship float?
questions.correct: Its hollow shape holds a lot of air
wrong: Steel is lighter than sea water
Its engines keep pushing it up
questions.explanation: With the air inside, the whole ship weighs less than the same volume of water, so it floats. If it fills with water, it sinks.

questions.question: Which temperature scale starts at absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature?
questions.explanation: Zero kelvin is the point where particles have almost no motion left. One kelvin step is the same size as one degree Celsius.

questions.question: A bicycle dynamo lights a lamp as the wheel spins. What energy change is this?
questions.explanation: A magnet spins inside a coil of wire and pushes electricity through it. That is why the lamp is dim when you ride very slowly.

questions.question: What happens to water pressure as you dive deeper?
questions.explanation: The deeper you go, the more water is above you pressing down. Submarines need strong hulls for this reason.

questions.question: What is absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, in degrees Celsius?
questions.explanation: The exact value is −273.15 °C, which is 0 kelvin. Nothing can be cooled below it, though laboratories have come very close.

questions.question: Which Danish physicist won the 1922 Nobel Prize for his work on the structure of atoms?
questions.explanation: Bohr suggested that electrons orbit the nucleus in fixed energy levels. His institute in Copenhagen became a world centre for atomic physics.

questions.question: Who showed in 1676, by watching the moons of Jupiter, that light takes time to travel?
questions.explanation: The Danish astronomer saw that eclipses of Jupiter's moon Io came later when Jupiter was further from Earth, because the light had further to go.

questions.question: Who discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831?
questions.explanation: Faraday found that moving a magnet near a wire makes electricity flow. This is how power-station generators work.

questions.question: Which Scottish physicist worked out in the 1860s that light is an electromagnetic wave?
questions.explanation: His equations joined electricity, magnetism and light in one theory. They also predicted radio waves, which Heinrich Hertz made in the late 1880s.

questions.question: Who discovered X-rays in 1895?
questions.explanation: Röntgen saw a screen glow near a covered tube and found that the new rays passed through flesh but not bone. He won the first Nobel Prize in Physics.

questions.question: What does the time of one swing of a pendulum mainly depend on?
questions.explanation: A longer pendulum swings more slowly. Galileo is said to have noticed that the size of the swing hardly matters while watching a lamp in Pisa Cathedral.

questions.question: Why does a skydiver stop speeding up and fall at a steady speed?
questions.explanation: As she speeds up, air pushes back harder. When the two forces are equal, she stops accelerating. This is terminal velocity.

questions.question: A car doubles its speed. How many times more kinetic energy does it have?
questions.explanation: Kinetic energy depends on speed squared. This is why braking distances grow so quickly at higher speeds.

questions.question: What makes the rainbow colours on a soap bubble?
questions.correct: Light waves interfering in the thin skin
questions.explanation: Light bounces off the front and back of the thin film and the two waves combine. Different thicknesses give different colours.

questions.question: Which British physicist discovered the electron in 1897?
questions.explanation: Thomson showed that cathode rays are tiny particles much lighter than atoms. They were later named electrons.

questions.question: For which work did Einstein win the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics?
questions.explanation: Einstein explained how light knocks electrons out of metal by treating light as packets of energy. This helped start quantum physics.

questions.question: Which German physicist is famous for the uncertainty principle?
questions.explanation: The principle says you cannot know both the exact position and the exact momentum of a tiny particle at the same time.

questions.question: In 1919, observers at a solar eclipse supported general relativity by measuring what?
questions.correct: The bending of starlight near the Sun
wrong: The heat of the Sun's corona
questions.explanation: Stars near the Sun appeared slightly out of place, as Einstein had predicted. The news made him world famous.

questions.question: A spinning football curves in flight. What is this effect called?
questions.explanation: Spin drags the air round the ball unevenly, so the air pushes harder on one side and the ball swerves. It is named after the German scientist Heinrich Magnus.

questions.question: Which law says that force equals mass times acceleration?
questions.explanation: A heavier object needs a bigger force to speed up by the same amount. This is why a loaded lorry is slow to start.

questions.question: A spring stretches twice as far when the pulling force is doubled. Whose law is this?
questions.explanation: Hooke's law works as long as the spring is not stretched too far. Spring balances use it to measure weight.

questions.question: Ohm's law links voltage, the flow of electricity and what?
questions.explanation: Voltage equals current times resistance. A higher resistance lets less current flow for the same voltage.

questions.question: What name is given to a metal shell that shields what is inside from electric fields?
questions.explanation: Charges spread over the outside of the metal and cancel the field inside. A car's metal body works a bit like this.

questions.question: What is it called when a heavy nucleus splits and gives out energy?
questions.explanation: Fission is used in nuclear power stations. Fusion, when light nuclei join, is how the Sun makes its energy.

questions.question: What effect keeps light inside an optical fibre as it travels along the glass thread?
questions.explanation: When light hits the edge of the glass at a shallow angle, all of it bounces back inside. Fibres carry internet signals this way.

questions.question: Water warms up slowly compared with most materials. What property explains this?
questions.explanation: It takes a lot of heat to raise water's temperature by one degree. This is why the sea stays cool in spring while land warms fast.

questions.question: You push a box with 10 newtons over 3 metres. How much work do you do?
questions.explanation: Work equals force times distance. One joule is the work of a one-newton force moving something one metre.

questions.question: A dropped stone near the Earth's surface speeds up each second by about what?
questions.explanation: Without air resistance, every falling object gains about 9.8 metres per second each second. This is called g.

questions.question: Which of these electromagnetic waves has the shortest wavelength?
questions.explanation: Gamma rays have the shortest waves and the most energy. Radio waves have the longest.

questions.question: How far behind a flat mirror does your image appear to be?
questions.correct: As far as you are in front of it
wrong: On the surface of the mirror
questions.explanation: Mirror images seem to sit behind the glass at the same distance. This is why a mirror in a small room makes it look bigger.

questions.question: If you double the distance between two masses, gravity between them becomes how much?
questions.explanation: Gravity follows an inverse-square law. Three times the distance makes it one ninth as strong.

questions.question: Which Italian invented the first electric battery around 1800?
questions.explanation: Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper with cloth soaked in salt water between them. The volt, the unit of voltage, is named after him.

questions.question: What happens to a magnet if it is heated strongly enough?
questions.explanation: Above a temperature called the Curie point, heat knocks its tiny atomic magnets out of line, so they no longer add up. For iron this is about 770 °C.

questions.question: In a vacuum flask, the empty space between the walls mainly stops what?
questions.correct: Heat moving by conduction and convection
wrong: The smell of the drink escaping
questions.explanation: Heat cannot cross empty space in these two ways. A shiny coating on the walls cuts down the radiation that is left.

questions.question: Which inventor is the SI unit of magnetic flux density named after?
questions.explanation: The tesla measures how strong a magnetic field is. Nikola Tesla is also known for his work on alternating-current (AC) motors.

questions.question: What is a particle of light called?
questions.explanation: Light travels as tiny packets of energy called photons. A phonon, by comparison, is a packet of vibration in a solid.

questions.question: Which physicist worked out that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus after his team fired particles at gold foil?
questions.explanation: Most particles passed straight through, but a few bounced back. This showed the atom is mostly empty space.

questions.question: What is the name for waves spreading out as they pass through a narrow gap or round an edge?
questions.explanation: Diffraction is why you can hear someone talking round a corner. Longer waves spread out more than short ones.

questions.question: When white light passes through a glass prism, which colour bends the most?
questions.explanation: Glass slows short waves more than long waves, so violet is bent the most. Red is bent the least.

questions.question: What do we call a material that carries electricity with no resistance when very cold?
questions.explanation: A current in a superconducting loop can keep flowing with no power supply. Superconductors make the strong magnets in many hospital scanners.

questions.question: A transformer works only with which kind of electricity?
questions.explanation: A changing current makes a changing magnetic field, which pushes current in a second coil. Transformers change voltage this way.

questions.question: A ball is thrown sideways at the same moment a second ball is dropped from the same height. Ignoring air, which lands first?
questions.correct: They land at the same time
questions.explanation: Sideways motion does not change how fast gravity pulls down. Both balls fall the same distance in the same time.

questions.question: Whose double-slit experiment in the early 1800s showed that light behaves like a wave?
questions.explanation: Light from two narrow slits made a pattern of light and dark stripes. Waves that add up and cancel each other out explain this pattern.

questions.question: A spinning skater pulls her arms in and spins faster. Which principle is this?
questions.explanation: Pulling her arms in brings her mass closer to the centre, so she must turn faster to keep the same angular momentum.
